description: Équipe FZKL (Foxtrot Zulu Kilo Lima). Focalisée sur l'ingénierie, l'analyse de données et le développement d'une solution optimisée pour le défi Lunar Landing Site Navigator.
summary:
SPHEREx Explorer is a public web tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Give it a star name or coordinates and it shows a short movie of what NASA's SPHEREx telescope saw there, visit after visit, so that anything that moved or changed brightness stands out. It works for any place in the sky, straight from the public archive, and the five test targets of the challenge load at once.

It goes further than a viewer. The service follows every source of a field by itself and lists the ones that moved or changed, with a speed, a distance when it can be measured, and a confidence. It measures the spectrum of an object on the fly across the 102 bands. The site opens on a map of the whole sky in SPHEREx colors, where a visitor chooses where to look, and a guided tour shows the way in twelve cards. A public journal collects what was found.

Every number the tool shows was checked against a catalog or a test that anyone can rerun. Pointed at the place of WISE 0855 with no hint, it finds the cold brown dwarf by itself, where the Gaia catalog holds nothing.
details:
Links

  • Site, which opens on the sky map: https://fzkl-spaceapps-2026.pages.dev
  • Explorer, on Barnard's Star: https://fzkl-spaceapps-2026.pages.dev/?target=barnard-star
  • Guided tour: https://fzkl-spaceapps-2026.pages.dev/sky?tour=1
  • Code: https://github.com/Yirmeyan/fzkl-spaceapps-2026
  • Service and its documentation: https://spherex-explorer-139331018511.us-east4.run.app/api/docs

What it does

  • A movie of any place. A name or coordinates in, the SPHEREx images of that place out, grouped by detector and by visit, so that what changes on screen is the sky and not the wavelength. Play, blink between the first and the last visit, subtract one visit from another, or stack a visit to bring out an object as faint as WISE 0855.
  • A spectrum on the fly. One request measures an object in every exposure that covers it, from 0.75 to 5 micrometers.
  • A search that runs by itself. The service follows every source of the field from visit to visit and lists the ones that moved or changed, with their speed, their distance when it can be measured, and a confidence. It also looks for a body of the outer solar system, which swings by tens of arcseconds with the seasons.
  • A map of the whole sky. The page the site opens on: the all-sky cube SPHEREx published in November 2026, in 99 wavelengths. A click on any place opens the tool there.
  • A journal. The 28 findings of our own checks, each with what catalogs say of it. A visitor who sees something adds a mark in one click: a place and a category, nothing to write, so nothing to moderate. The journal says what each visitor saw: it moves, it changes brightness, it appears once, or something else.
  • Other telescopes. Gaia DR3 stars drawn over the image at the date of each frame, and AllWISE objects where WISE saw them in 2010, with a legend. A star that has left its 2010 place stands out.
  • A link for everything. The address of the page holds the place and the view, so the tool can be embedded or shared. Every visit starts with a short introduction and a guided tour in twelve cards, from the sky map to the running film, where the visitor only presses Next. A sentence under each button says what it does.

How it works

A static site and a small Python service. SPHEREx has no filter wheel: the wavelength an object is seen at changes at every exposure, so the tool compares images of the same detector, visit against visit. A file weighs 62 MB and a view needs about 60 of them: the service reads only the bytes it needs in the public files, about 1 percent of each. It computes where a moving target was at the date of each exposure. Nothing is copied ahead of time for other places, so a new data release is one setting.

What we checked

Nobody gave us the expected answers, so each step was checked against something independent.

  • Flux. On 8 steady stars, the median of measured over catalog (2MASS, AllWISE) is 0.998.
  • Spectra. Against the published SPIFF library, the median ratio is 1.016 over 297 bands.
  • Motion. 16 of 17 nearby stars are found with no position given, each speed within two sigma of its catalog. 32 quiet fields give no candidate.
  • Faint limit. 2,560 made-up stars were added to real frames. One that moves by 3 arcseconds per year is found nine times in ten from 0.3 millijansky.
  • Planet X. 1,344 made-up bodies were hidden in real frames, between 1,600 and 24,000 astronomical units. 79 percent of those of 1 millijansky were found.
  • Honesty. One blind round on 21 fields chosen before the run gave one false alarm, since corrected. The service has 634 automated tests and the site 103.

Limits

SPHEREx has observed for less than two years: most places have two to four visits. A star that is too bright saturates, and the tool says so instead of showing a wrong number. What the search lists are candidates, not discoveries.

Use of AI

We used AI as a tool, and we say where.

  • Most of the code, the tests and the documentation were written by AI assistants directed by the team. Claude, by Anthropic, for the service, the data pipeline, the sky map, the guided tour and the last simplifications of the interface. Cursor Agent for the explorer page.
  • The idea and the decisions are the team's: the choice of the challenge, the priorities, the architecture, what to build and what to drop.
  • Every scientific claim comes from a check that can be rerun, not from what a model remembers.
  • No image or video is generated. Every picture the tool shows is SPHEREx data.
  • The texts of this page and the demo slides were drafted with Claude and reviewed by the team. The pictures of the slides are captures of the tool.
  • The same statement travels with the code: in the README, in the metadata of the Python package, in the description of the service, and in a metadata tag of every page of the site.

References

Papers: Bock et al. 2026, ApJ 999, 139 (the SPHEREx mission). Akeson et al. 2026, ApJS 285, 67 (the pipeline). Korngut et al. 2026, arXiv:2603.29835 (the instrument). Luhman 2014, ApJ 781, 4. Rice and Laughlin 2020, PSJ 1, 81. Bertin and Arnouts 1996, A&AS 117, 393: the windowed positions our source centers follow, written again, no code taken.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, pydantic-settings, httpx2, NumPy, Astropy, pytest, Ruff, uv and Hatchling for the service. React, Vite, TypeScript, Biome and Vitest for the site, with the fonts IBM Plex Sans and Syne. Aladin Lite for the sky map. Google Cloud Run and Firestore, Cloudflare Pages and GitHub Actions for hosting. Every source and dependency, with its license: docs/sources.md in the repository.
